nameStory: The Northern Blood Star gets its dramatic name from its most common coloration - a rich, blood-red hue that makes it look like a crimson jewel on the ocean floor. The scientific name 'sanguinolenta' literally means 'bloody' in Latin, reinforcing this striking visual characteristic. While it can come in other colors, that deep red variety clearly made the strongest impression on early naturalists!
description: The Northern Blood Star is a stunning sea star that crawls along the rocky bottom of New England's cold coastal waters. This elegant five-armed starfish typically displays vibrant colors ranging from deep blood-red to bright orange, sunny yellow, rich purple, or soft lavender. Its arms are relatively long and slender compared to many other sea stars, giving it a graceful, delicate appearance. You'll find these beautiful creatures in deeper waters, usually below the low tide line.

idTips.label: Vibrant coloration
idTips.description: Look for brilliant solid colors - deep red, bright orange, yellow, purple, or lavender - with a smooth, almost velvety texture to the skin

idTips.label: Five slender arms
idTips.description: Arms are relatively long and tapered, feeling firm but slightly flexible when gently touched, not thick and chunky like some sea stars

idTips.label: Smooth surface texture
idTips.description: The surface feels smooth and soft to the touch, lacking the obvious spines or bumpy texture of many other sea star species

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Medium-sized sea star with arms that are noticeably longer in proportion to the central disc compared to chunky species like cushion stars

idTips.label: Deep water habitat
idTips.description: Usually found in deeper water on rocky or hard surfaces, rarely in shallow tide pools where you'd see common sea stars

habitat: Northern Blood Stars live in the deeper, colder waters off New England's rocky coastlines, typically below the low tide line. They prefer hard surfaces like rocks, ledges, and shells where they can grip firmly with their tube feet. You're most likely to encounter them while diving or in deeper tide pools during extremely low tides, rather than in the shallow pools where common sea stars are easily found.

seasonality.spring: Active in deeper waters as temperatures begin to warm. Best spotted during exceptionally low spring tides that expose normally submerged rocky areas.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're feeding and moving across the seafloor. Divers and snorkelers have the best chance of spotting them during this season.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Late fall diving may reveal them on exposed rocky ledges.
seasonality.winter: Present but less active in the coldest months. They retreat to deeper, more stable waters but can occasionally be found during winter diving.

funFact: Northern Blood Stars are incredibly long-lived and can regenerate not just lost arms, but an entire new sea star can grow from just a single severed arm as long as it contains part of the central disc - essentially making them nearly immortal if they avoid predators!
confusionNotes: The Northern Blood Star looks nearly identical to its close relative "Bloody Henry" (Henricia oculata) - so similar that scientists need laboratory tests to tell them apart! In the field, just enjoy spotting a beautiful Henricia blood star without worrying about which exact species you're seeing.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "starfish," blood stars aren't fish at all - they're echinoderms, more closely related to sea urchins and sand dollars. The term "sea star" is preferred by marine biologists to avoid this confusion.
compareHints: Since the Northern Blood Star is the only Henricia species reliably identified in New England waters, compare it to other colorful sea stars in the region. Unlike the chunky, short-armed cushion stars or the spiny, textured surfaces of common sea stars, blood stars have that distinctive smooth, velvety feel and elegant proportions. Their vibrant, solid coloration and graceful form make them the supermodels of the New England sea star world.
